entries.title: Lisa Cook Turns Mortgage Fraud Accusations Back on Trump and Bessent
entries.summary: Several recent reports allege that the president has engaged in the same activity he’s accused Cook of.
entries.content:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook is hitting back at the Trump administration’s second attempt to oust her by pointing out that the president has reportedly engaged in the same activity she’s being accused of.

The White House has said Cook committed mortgage fraud by claiming multiple primary residences on her taxes, an accusation it has deemed serious enough to warrant her ouster from the Fed board. Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. In a Wednesday letter to the White House, her counsel pointed to a number of recent news stories that found President Donald Trump and multiple Cabinet members appear to have done the same — without facing any repercussions.

“Surely the President does not believe himself ‘unfit for office’ because he signed these contradictory ‘primary’ mortgage documents,” Cook’s letter says.

The letter is a response to Trump’s second attempt to remove Cook, a Biden appointee, from the seven-person board, which kicked off with a letter on Aug. 5, giving her 21 days to respond to the allegation. Trump has appointed three of the current governors, but the Supreme Court ruled in June that the president couldn’t remove Cook while her lawsuit challenging the termination continued.

Trump has used accusations of mortgage fraud to try to oust Cook and New York Attorney General Letitia James, but multiple news outlets have reported that administration members have also claimed multiple primary residences.

For example, Trump got two mortgages for Florida homes in 1993 that he claimed would be his principal residence, according to ProPublica.

“President Trump’s two mortgages you are referencing are from the same lender,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement to ProPublica. “There was no defraudation. It is illogical to believe that the same lender would agree to defraud itself.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Attorney General Todd Blanche have also claimed multiple primary home mortgages at the same time.

“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Cook’s counsel Abbe D. Lowell said in a statement Wednesday. “These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will. Our response should put this matter to rest once and for all, but, if necessary and in keeping with the Supreme Court’s ruling, we are prepared to challenge any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.”

The White House and Justice and Treasury departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Trump Appoints Longtime Ally to Lead Agency Overseeing His Construction Projects
entries.summary: Mark Paoletta, a lawyer who also served in the first Trump administration, will inherit a number of embattled construction projects.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump appointed Mark Paoletta, a federal government official with at least three other administration positions, to lead the planning commission tasked with reviewing the White House’s many construction projects, Paoletta confirmed in a statement.

Paoletta, the conservative lawyer who helped gut the federal bureaucracy as a deputy to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, is set to inherit a number of legally contentious initiatives such as the White House ballroom, the 250-foot triumphal arch and the installation of permanent fencing on Pennsylvania Avenue.

Paoletta said he was “honored” to be appointed by Trump as at-large commissioner and chairman of the National Capital Planning Commission. The NCPC’s website was updated as of Thursday to reflect the leadership change.

“President Trump has transformed DC into a Capital worthy of the greatest nation in history,” Paoletta said. “I look forward to working with my new colleagues to further the president’s historic restoration and beautification of the National Capital Region, especially in the 250th year of our country’s independence.”

He will succeed Will Scharf, who will transition to a new job as White House counsel beginning Sept. 1.

Paoletta, who Trump once deemed a “conservative warrior,” has been a close ally to the president since his first term in office. His other roles currently include general counsel for OMB and acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He also performs the duties of administrator of OMB’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, a federal office that reviews government regulations.

Trump has made D.C. beautification projects a priority since his return to office, despite opposition from local elected officials and preservation groups. The projects have faced a series of setbacks, such as botched renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool that led to peeling paint and internal disputes over vandalism charges.

The Interior Department has spent nearly $95 million in taxpayer funds on renovations between December 2025 and April 2026.

entries.title: Edwards Sends Letter Refuting Ethics Censure: 'Poetry Is Not Sexual Misconduct'
entries.summary: The North Carolina Republican maintains his relationships with female staffers were friendships and not sexual harassment.
entries.content:
Embattled North Carolina Rep. Chuck Edwards sent a 22-page letter to his colleagues defending himself against sexual harassment allegations that led to his decision to not run for reelection in November.

The letter follows a report from the House Ethics Committee that found there was “substantial evidence” to believe that Edwards engaged in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” The panel recommended that the North Carolina congressman be censured as a result of the investigation. The full House could vote next month on the punishment, which would require Edwards to stand in the chamber as the resolution condemning his behavior is read aloud.

“An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition. A gift is not sexual misconduct. A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct. Socializing with a colleague is not sexual misconduct. Caring deeply about someone with whom you have worked and come to know for years is not sexual misconduct,” Edwards wrote in the letter, which was obtained by NOTUS.

Edwards distributed the letter to members via text group chats, according to a source familiar with the matter.

Multiple staffers testified to the House Ethics Committee that they felt uncomfortable during an incident in which Edwards read a poem he wrote for a staffer that was leaving his office. He cried while reading the poem, according to the panel’s report.

In the letter, which NOTUS obtained, Edwards said the committee found “that I neither engaged in sexual activity with nor explicitly propositioned any individual staff member.” He also said there is “no House rule prohibiting members and staff from being friends” or “spending social time together” or “genuinely and deeply caring about” each other.

“Friendship is not misconduct. Generosity is not misconduct. Social interaction is not misconduct. Caring deeply about colleagues who have become important parts of your life is not misconduct,” Edwards said.

“Conduct does not become sexual harassment merely because someone looking backward through thousands of pages can construct a theory under which is ‘could be interpreted as romantic,’” he added.

Under the current rules of the House of Representatives, members are prohibited from having romantic or sexual relationships with any employee directly under their supervision. Lawmakers are also prohibited from engaging in “unwelcome sexual advances or conduct” toward any House employee.

The Ethics Committee concluded that two of Edwards’ female staffers “received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.” Edwards, 65, has been married since 1980.

The panel said that one of the staffers stated that she felt “obligated to wear” a necklace Edwards gave her, and the congressman told her he was disappointed when she did not wear it.

Edwards also claimed that he not only gave gifts to female staffers, but also gifted male employees “olive oil, wine, cookware, rum, Kennedy Center tickets and even a handgun to a male employee.”

The letter says he testified that one female employee referred to him as her “second dad” and that he “knows the committee received other testimony from another witness who worked closely with us for years and who viewed another of these relationships as a father/daughter and mentor/mentee relationship.”

A spokesperson for Edwards did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The story was updated to correct the letter was 22 pages, not 23.

entries.title: Meta Millions
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 27, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Big tech is set to pay D.C. some big bucks. Meta will pay the District between $90 million and $130 million over the next decade to resolve a large, multistate lawsuit that accused the company of knowingly endangering children’s mental health.

The settlement is among the largest consumer-protection payouts in the city’s history, NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright reports. The tech giant will fork over up to $17 billion to dozens of states and U.S. territories. It’s a massive sum, but one that amounts to just 1% of the company’s stock value.

In addition to the money — and maybe more significantly — Meta agreed to stricter protections for teenage users of Facebook and Instagram, including hard time limits, limits on night usage and better controls over potentially harmful content.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb, who sued the company in 2023, said those safeguards will “fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook.”

So how will D.C. spend its share of the settlement? That’s unclear, but at least half must go toward mental health support or enrichment for young people. That investment could include boosting funds for the 988 crisis hotline, funding more outdoors and sports programs for teens, or adding digital literacy counselors to schools.

In the wake of Wednesday’s agreement, Meta is aggressively encouraging competitors TikTok and YouTube to establish similar protective measures for teens. That PR push involves full-page print ads in The New York Times, Washington Post and Los Angeles Times,according to The New York Times’ Mike Issac.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A D.C. man was arrested for filming federal immigration agents as they detained someone behind his home in Northwest, reports WUSA9. The man said he was not interfering and was knocked over by a D.C. police officer, who later arrested him. He spent the night in jail, though his charges were later dropped.

D.C. is home to the world’s only liberal arts university dedicated to the deaf community: Gallaudet University. But not every student shows up knowing American Sign Language. A three-week bootcamp at the start of the school year helps them learn, The Washington Post reports.

Return to sender: A growing number of working, would-be homebuyers in D.C. are living with their parents while they save up for their own place, Axios D.C. reports.

D.C.’s only cookbook store, Bold Fork Books in Mount Pleasant, announced it will close next month, citing economic pressures, City Cast D.C. reports.

The food hall startup Wonder is planning to have 30 locations in the DMV by the end of the year, making the region one of the food tech company’s fastest-growing markets, Axios D.C. reports.





TALK TO TOM

DC0A8329 copy.jpg (10898x7812, AR: 1.40)
Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

I’m looking for a solid restaurant with a view in the city. 

Look no further than Limani, the dashing, three-floor Greek oasis whose picture windows capture boats, water and more at The Wharf in Southwest D.C. The airy white interior with accents of blue makes me feel cooler just walking in, and I appreciate the consistency of the cooking. When opening executive chef Lonnie Zoeller died unexpectedly last year, his sous chef, Antonio Contreras, ably slipped into his place in the kitchen.

A meal this month reminded me of my first visit to Limani. Fried in a kettle of olive oil, the signature stack of thin, hand-cut eggplant and zucchini arrives glossy but greaseless — also hot, crisp and cooled with a dip of tzatziki. (Move over, potato chips.) Bite into the supple grilled squid and out rushes a river of tangy cheese. Loup de mer is cooked head-on, then simply brightened with capers and lemon. A trio of lamb chops is as succulent as I remember, too, and don’t be surprised when a server in a white jacket delivers a gratis gift to the table. (My party received a strawberry pavlova to share.)

In the full Q&A: Server etiquette, well-designed menus and a new spot for a good but casual meal. 





SPORTS

Training camp update: The Commanders made the short trip to Baltimore on Wednesday for a joint practice with the Ravens, and NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that it did not go well.

Washington has injuries on both sides of the ball right now, but it was the offense that looked especially bad in Baltimore. Jayden Daniels was pressured and running backs were stuffed as the team struggled to move the ball. It was an ominous performance with less than three weeks remaining before Week 1.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Rockies, 1:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics at Mercury, 10 p.m. (Amazon Prime)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS.

entries.title: Postmarked by Never?
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The Postal Service may not be able to deliver Trump’s mail-in package. Using AI to decide your vote. Jamie Raskin readies his investigation list. And: How easy is it to rename things “America”?





THE LATEST

Donald Trump’s plan to employ the U.S. Postal Service to screen voters for eligibility for mailed ballots in this year’s midterms is tied up in court battles. But even if — and that’s still a big IF — all the legal wrangling were resolved and the Trump administration prevailed at the Supreme Court, with less than 70 days until the election, the Postal Service has little time to figure out how to deliver a system to check ballots against state-provided voter rolls.

Some postage-paid ballots from county clerks could land at local post offices in weeks. And any screwups in the yet-to-exist system, even assuming a small error rate, could disenfranchise a lot of voters. It’s way more complicated than getting your impulse-purchased Amazon package that last mile; a late or denied delivery here could prompt an election-wide fiasco.

“This is not something where you just flip the switch and turn it on,” Tom Day, a Postal Service executive for 35 years, told NOTUS’ Eric Katz, who penned a detailed look at how Trump’s mail-in ballot plan may not arrive on time. “I don’t know how the hell they’re going to do it.”

The Postal Service would normally spend a year to roll out a system like this, Day said, and push educational efforts for the tens of thousands of postal clerks across the country. “To do it in three weeks,” he said, “my God, there’s no way.”

Open tabs: Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement (Stateline); House GOP leaders eye quick vote on Senate-passed stopgap (Politico); Maryland Judge Strikes Down Democratic Redistricting Ballot Measure (NOTUS); Years Late, Billions Over Budget: California’s High-Speed Rail Hasn’t Laid a Track (WSJ); U.S. weapons shortage from Iran war alarms allies confronting China (WaPo)





From the campaign trail


Hey, Grok, who should I vote for? A recent study shared exclusively with NOTUS looked at how voters might be using AI chatbots to answer political questions, including which candidates they should support, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider writes. Some Democratic strategists are warning their campaigns not to ignore the answers. Artificial intelligence apps, to our dismay, aren’t just using news sites for info but rather leaning on campaign website pages, YouTube interviews and a candidate’s digital footprint.

From the Hill


Request to revoke: California Democratic Party delegates are circulating a petition urging the state party to rescind its endorsement of Rep. Jimmy Gomez as he faces a sexual misconduct investigation by the House Ethics Committee, NOTUS’ Oriana González tells us. The petition, which has been signed by more than 50 state delegates, including 11 from Gomez’s district, comes as the Ethics Committee is days away from hitting a 60-day preelection blackout period that would bar it from releasing any findings ahead of the midterms.

On notice: Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, is lining up his focus in case Democrats reclaim the majority, NOTUS’ Jose Pagliery reports. Last week, Raskin sent letters to U.S. attorneys in five districts, including D.C.’s Jeanine Pirro, warning that he’s investigating whether DOJ attorneys misled judges.







NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Dana Milbank scrutinized the Republican Party’s message on inflation as the midterms approach. He found that it boils down to: Stop whining!





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: D.C. Could Receive Up to $130M From Meta as Part of Massive Settlement, by Jenny Gathright

Talk to Tom: A Great Tavern-Style Pizza Joint in Dupont, by Tom Sietsema

Sports desk: The Commanders Have Their Offensive Issues Exposed in Joint Practice, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

Nomenclatural considerations: Earlier this week, Trump threatened to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” But is that even possible? NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal writes that in essence, yes.

Normally, the U.S. Board on Geographic Names takes months or years to review name-change requests. But, Dave writes, when Trump signed an executive order last year mandating the “Gulf of Mexico” be renamed the “Gulf of America,” he upended that entire process and it moved rapidly. Trump threatened to do it again this week.

But even if the name is legally changed, Dave writes, Trump cannot force anyone to use the name, even if he really, really wants to. One such example — all the local jurisdictions that have already defied the president, including Florida residents who voted to keep their “Gulf of Mexico Drive.”

More: The Senate’s NATO Backstop Is About to Lose Its Biggest Champions, by Hamed Ahmadi

A Judge Says Texas Authorities Can Release an ICE Agent Who Shot a Man by Jose Pagliery

Pentagon Claims Hegseth’s Afghanistan Withdrawal Probe Found ‘Hidden’ Files, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

AOC Officially Rejoins DSA as 2028 Speculation Heats Up, by Jenna Monnin

Josh Shapiro and RFK Jr. Trade Barbs Over Deadly Measles Outbreak, by Torrie Herrington

Rep. Beatty Says Trump Is Using Mob-Like Tactics in Kennedy Center Battle, by Torrie Herrington





NOT US

  • Everyone is making a U-turn on data centers as public support craters, by Andrew Howard for Politico
  • In Virginia’s Navy Country, the Iran War Tests a G.O.P. Incumbent, by Olivia Diaz for The New York Times
  • Before Hegseth fired him, top general was advised to drop Kid Rock probe, by Dan Lamothe and Noah Robertson for The Washington Post

entries.title: Democrats Are Getting Some Answers to Their Chatbot Problems
entries.summary: New research from a Democratic-aligned firm estimates chatbots get 650,000 questions about politics every week.
entries.content:
Democrats insist their campaigns need to take AI chatbots seriously. And now some think they have early answers for how to actually make that happen.

A recent study, commissioned by Democratic-aligned public relations firm Orchestra and shared first with NOTUS, analyzed how voters use large language models to extract information about candidates and issues — a new digital frontier where the parties will battle for primacy. The research, conducted by the AI-marketing platform Evertune, estimated that chatbots are asked 650,000 prompts about politics weekly, primarily through ChatGPT and Google AI.

Chatbots, and how voters use them, are injecting a complicating dimension into campaign digital strategy this year. It’s another way to target voters, strategists from both parties acknowledge, and they’re racing to figure out how to influence the information those AI-generated bots spit out. In 2024, early iterations of these chatbots pumped out false and misleading data on voting, raising more warnings for both parties.

“The best campaigns are usually the ones that have the best sense of how the electorate is living their lives and receiving and sharing content and information at that moment and do their best to mirror it in their own resourcing and approach,” said David Plouffe, who advised the project. “LLM now joins the stage with Tiktok, Instagram and YouTube as a core challenge and opportunity for campaigns to navigate and master.”

Chatbots won’t forecast a winner or endorse a candidate, the study found when it tested those questions. But when asked about the candidates generally, their platforms and campaign promises, that’s when the quality of a candidates’ digital footprint became more clear.

In one test case, the researchers compared the AI-generated answers for the policy positions of Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and GOP Rep. Mike Collins for their hotly contested Senate race, where it found Ossoff’s easy-to-read and well-annotated campaign issues pages gave him the upper hand in generating citations. “Answer engines repeatedly return to Ossoff pages,” the research found, because they were “detailed” and “clearly labeled.”

But Republicans hold an advantage on their economic storytelling through chatbots, the study found — a key issue for the midterms, which have been dominated by cost-of-living concerns. Through repeated engagement with the chatbots, the Republican economic pitch, centered on producing more energy coupled with reducing the cost of government, is more coherent than Democrats’, the study said. Democratic arguments are “fragmented,” as the models “do not consistently assemble them into the same overarching account,” the study said.

“When a party frames an issue consistently across campaign content, official records and media coverage, models are more likely to reproduce it coherently,” the study said. “If the response sounds scattered, the model may be reflecting deeper communications problems: the lack of a consistent message, the lack of a sufficient paper trail supporting that message — or both.”

Out of the AI-generated answers it tested, the study found chatbots predominately cite news coverage, but the “strongest URL” references were explainers, both from news outlets and partisan sources, like party platforms and campaign websites. The study urged campaigns to clarify their own candidates’ digital presence on issue-specific topics as a way to influence those answers.

It also found that YouTube clips of previous interviews or coverage — once seen as a one-off news cycle hit that doesn’t live beyond a single day — can take on new life through AI-generated answers through chatbots, which frequently cited those videos.

The study laid out other advice to campaigns: Treat campaign websites as resources, not just fundraising hubs and create content that “starts with a problem,” the same way a voter interacts with a chatbot.
entries.author: Elena Schneider

entries.title: Rep. Ashley Hinson's Husband 'Arranged' a Meeting Between Lobbyists and Iowa Lawmakers — Including His Wife
entries.summary: Hinson’s Senate campaign says she and her husband "maintain the highest ethical standards."
entries.content:
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, a congresswoman pitching herself as a warrior against special interests in Iowa, and her husband, Matt Arenholz, have deep ties to the insurance industry, with Arenholz owning millions worth of interest in a private equity-backed brokerage.

Documents reviewed by NOTUS reveal Arenholz also held a government affairs post at a leading insurance industry lobbying group, which has not been previously reported. He helped arrange meetings with Hinson and other Iowa congressional delegation members, the documents indicate.

Arenholz, a longtime insurance executive, chaired the government affairs committee for an Iowa branch of the Independent Insurance Agents & Brokers of America, an expansive national insurance trade association and lobbying group. Magazines published by the organization and reviewed by NOTUS reveal that officials at the insurance industry group credited Arenholz for helping them gain access to Hinson and other Iowa lawmakers.

“In fact, Matt was able to arrange a meeting with all four of our congressional members in one large conference room,” Tom O’Meara, the group’s chief executive officer, wrote in the message in the magazine. “This not only saved us a lot of time but prevented us from having to bounce around from building to building in D.C.”

O’Meara also acknowledged Hinson and Arenholz’s marriage in a fall 2023 edition of the group’s magazine. Archived material from the Independent Insurance Agents of Iowa’s website shows Arenholz took on the government affairs role with the group in 2019, and that he still held the post in 2023.

A spokesperson for the Hinson campaign, which is competing in one of the nation’s hottest Senate races, told NOTUS the meeting O’Meara referenced was “arranged just like any other meeting with an advocacy group is arranged through the proper and appropriate channels.”

The spokesperson, who declined to be identified by name for this story, said Arenholz has been a part of the Iowa insurance organization since 2003, and that his government affairs post was focused on state level issues. The panel, the campaign said, meets once a year and hears from state lobbyists about the Iowa state legislative session.

“Matt’s not a lobbyist nor has he ever lobbied Ashley on anything — they maintain the highest ethical standards,” the Hinson campaign spokesperson said. The Hinson spokesperson also said the congresswoman understood Arenholz’s involvement with the organization to be part of his participation in the broader independent insurance industry.

The Independent Insurance Agents of Iowa did not respond to a request for comment or questions about Arenholz’s role at the organization.

In a copy of the organization's online magazine, O’Meara wrote that while in Washington for a conference, he was asked how many members of Iowa’s congressional delegation met with his organization.

“I was given several strange looks when I responded that we met with all six of ours from Iowa,” O’Meara wrote. “Several replied to me that they were not talking about congressional staff members rather the actual elected officials themselves. My answer remained the same, ALL SIX!”

Jeff Hauser, executive director of the Revolving Door Project, a watchdog organization that tracks lobbying and political influence trends, told NOTUS that Arenholz’s position “blurs the line.”

“No one’s saying that if your significant other gets elected to Congress, you have got to stop being in insurance,” Hauser said. “Then you tell me he’s involved in government affairs, right off the bat that’s not normal. Most people don’t do government affairs work.”

Hauser argued that national organizations such as the Independent Insurance Agent Brokers, the parent group of the Iowa-based branch, use a network of state-level offshoots to more effectively lobby lawmakers.

“Part of the power that, like, a Chamber of Commerce builds over time is that they can, instead of having their D.C-based official lobby someone from Iowa, they give talking points through their Iowa affiliate, and then the lobbying occurs from a constituent,” Hauser said.

InsurePAC, the political action committee of the Independent Insurance Agents & Brokers of America, has supported Hinson throughout her congressional career.

Over the years, the PAC contributed a total of more than $67,000 to Hinson’s campaign and PACs affiliated with the Iowa Republican, according to data from the Federal Election Commission. 

Separately, the national group has spent more than $5 million lobbying the federal government since Hinson was elected in 2020, according to Lobbying Disclosure Act reports.

A Hinson spokesperson said the support from the PAC “had no relationship to her husband’s membership” in the Iowa insurance group.

Hinson’s annual personal financial disclosures reveal Arenholz retains a significant stake in the insurance sector. Hinson reported in 2025 that Arenholz held between $1 million and $5 million in High Street Insurance Partners, a large private equity-backed insurance brokerage. In 2021, Hinson reported that Arenholz sold interest in a private insurance company for over $1 million.

Hinson has pitched herself in Iowa as a candidate who will take on powerful special interests.

In the first ad for her Senate campaign, Hinson said, “Health care companies are ripping you off, and members of Congress should not trade stocks.”

“I’m working with President Trump to take on big insurance companies, and I’m fighting to ban stock trading in Congress,” Hinson said in the ad.

The race for Senate in Iowa, with Hinson facing off against Democrat Josh Turek, has unexpectedly become one of the most important political contests in the 2026 midterms.

Hinson holds a polling advantage of less than 1 percentage point, according to polling averages from RealClearPolitics, meaning the race is a statistical dead heat, at present.

Last week, the Cook Political Report rated the Iowa Senate race a toss-up, shifting its rating toward Democrats. Senate Democrats must hold all of their seats and defeat at least four Republicans to retake the chamber.
entries.author: Stephen Neukam

entries.title: The Senate’s NATO Backstop Is About to Lose Its Biggest Champions
entries.summary: The retirements of Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Thom Tillis could spell trouble for the Senate NATO Observer Group.
entries.content:
Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Thom Tillis spent eight years rebuilding a bipartisan Senate channel to NATO at a time when allies increasingly looked to Congress for stability in Washington.

Now both are leaving Congress, with no successors settled and no guarantee the group they rebuilt will survive or carry the same weight without them.

Both senators say they are trying to keep the Senate NATO Observer Group, or SNOG, active. But neither gets to choose who takes over.

“It's not my decision. It's not Sen. Tillis's decision. It's the leadership's decision,” Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire, told NOTUS in an interview.

Their departure comes as the United States’ relationship with NATO is being tested under President Donald Trump.

Trump has pushed NATO allies to dramatically increase their defense spending, helping secure a new pledge last year for each nation to spend at least 5% of GDP by 2035. His second term has also deepened strains with the alliance, from renewed pressure for the U.S. to take over Greenland, clashes with European governments over the Iran war and moves to reduce the U.S. military presence in Europe.

Tillis described the group as a way for senators to reassure allies when Trump’s rhetoric raises doubts about the U.S.’s commitment to NATO.

“Look, you got to deal with the rhetoric. But the reality is, membership in NATO is a treaty that the president can certainly cause problems, but cannot by himself negate.” Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said in an interview.

Rachel Ellehuus, a former U.S. defense adviser at NATO, said the Senate group is “even more important now when we're getting mixed messages from the executive branch.”

“A group like the SNOG really does show you where that consensus is and reminds Europeans that there are representatives on both sides of the political aisle who strongly support NATO,” said Ellehuus, now the director-general of Royal United Services Institute, a U.K. defense think tank.

Over the years, the group became a regular presence at NATO summits and other major transatlantic gatherings, giving senators direct access to allied leaders and another way to signal bipartisan support. Most recently, Shaheen led a bipartisan delegation to the July summit in Ankara, Turkey, which her office described as her final one as co-chair.

Both senators pointed to Finland’s and Sweden’s NATO accessions as major accomplishments, saying the group helped build Senate support and move the ratification process quickly after Russia invaded Ukraine.

But the group has a built-in weakness: It does not formally exist in law. It is voluntary and has repeatedly come and gone since the Senate first created it in 1997 during NATO enlargement. Shaheen and Tillis revived it again in 2018.

That history is part of why Shaheen and Tillis are trying to make the group permanent before they leave, creating a clearer structure for succession and avoiding another lapse.

The senators introduced legislation last year to codify the group, but the bill has not advanced. Tillis said he still hopes to move it through the National Defense Authorization Act or a year-end package.

“I think it'd be ideal,” Tillis said. “I'm trying to do it ahead of leaving.”

Tillis said part of the holdup is an internal Senate dispute over who should control the group. He said no one is opposed to its existence, but some senators want to determine which committees its leaders should come from, something he called “silly or petty.”

“We've got some people in the mix that want to lead it or kind of fold it into one committee or another, which makes no sense,” Tillis said.

Without a permanent structure, the group depends heavily on its leaders, making its future influence largely a question of who takes over. Shaheen said she and Tillis “have had a really good relationship and share the same perspective about NATO.”

“When these groups have fallen to the wayside, it's because leaders have not invested the time,” Tillis said, adding that the group’s success is “very much personality-driven.”

“They're all as good as the commitment of the leaders, their working relationship, their ability to get other members engaged and their willingness to travel,” he added.

Jim Townsend, a former senior Pentagon official who also served in the U.S. Mission to NATO in Brussels, said Shaheen and Tillis “leave very big shoes to fill” because of their credibility on both sides of the Atlantic and the time they have invested in NATO relationships.

Tillis and Shaheen have both pointed to Sens. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and Angus King (I-Maine) as potential successors. Shaheen said Rounds and King “would be great,” but again stressed that the choice belongs to leadership. King’s office declined to comment on the matter.

Tillis has personally encouraged Rounds to consider the role and called him “probably first among all Republicans in his participation.”

Rounds said he is interested.

“I've indicated that I would like an opportunity to do that if it works into the bigger picture of where everybody else fits in,” he told NOTUS.

Rounds said he would be open to working with King but noted that other names have also been suggested. He said Senate leadership has not approached him about taking over.

Rounds said the next co-chairs will have to preserve the group’s bipartisan identity if they want it to have credibility overseas.

Congressional engagement carries real weight with allies because it gives them “another view about how Washington thinks” beyond the presidential administration, Townsend said.

Townsend said the group’s disappearance would leave a real gap in Congress’ NATO outreach.

“If the SNOG goes away, that takes a tool out of the toolbox,” Townsend said. “And if you don't have a SNOG providing that kind of voice, that will certainly hurt the effort to keep the alliance going through this tough time.”
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Talk to Tom: A Great Tavern-Style Pizza Joint in Dupont
entries.summary: Plus: What makes a well-designed menu, and a Greek restaurant with stunning views.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

Help me refresh my restaurant rotation. What’s good (but casual) these days?

“Good” and “casual” apply to the new La Merna in Dupont Circle — as does “tough to book.” On Friday night, I watched a steady stream of would-be customers politely turned away at the door of the 50-seat storefront.

That’s what happens when a couple of Chicago talents — chef Bradley Shorten and his wife, Meg Schmitt, a cheesemaker — come to town and open a place that features tavern-style pizza in a room that looks as if it had been airlifted from the Midwest. Faux pheasants, wood panelling, burgundy-colored banquettes and a small custom-made bar were inspired by the dive bars, supper clubs and old-school Italian restaurants familiar to the couple back home.

If you’re new to the genre, tavern-style pizza is defined by a thin, cracker-y crust that’s always cut in a grid pattern, squares being easier to eat off a cocktail napkin, which is how early tavern-style pies were dispatched in bars, bowling alleys and elsewhere. The subtle sour note in the base comes from curing, says Shorten. “By the time [the crust] gets to you, it’s a week old.”

Depending upon where you eat the pizza, the tomato sauce can be sweet or spicy. La Merna’s sauce reflects the zesty variety served on Chicago’s North Side, says Shorten, who gets a “good forearm workout” from the sausage he mixes by hand.

The cheerful service places you in the Midwest, too. “We ask [hires] to make everybody feel like a regular,” says Schmitt, who makes the pasta for the restaurant, which is named for her grandmother’s best friend and neighbor. “My favorite person in the world,” adds Schmitt. A painting of the late inspiration graces the first-come, first-serve bar, the source of some top-shelf drinks.

Reservations open 30 days out, at midnight. The best time to drop by is when the doors open at 5 p.m. or late at night, say the couple, who are just getting started. A quarter of their ideas, including (yes!) late-night burgers, have yet to go on the menu. Right now, in addition to the signature pies, I’m partial to the mile-high Italian chopped salad and floppy ravioli plumped with ricotta, draped with tangy tomato sauce and scattered with crispy bread crumbs spiked with ’nduja.

When you’re looking at a menu for the first time, what captures your attention? 

Lots of things!

I appreciate a list that’s concise, which certainly fits the times now. Don’t give me dozens of options. It’s the uncommon kitchen that can produce a lot successfully. Generally speaking, eight or so appetizers and as many main course options suggest a chef has done some editing — and thinking, and paring — for a diner by putting forth their best work.

I also commend a menu that provides enough of a description to give patrons a sense of what the dish will taste like. I’m not asking for a complete recipe, mind you, just more than three or four words, as I’ve seen in some contemporary restaurants.

A menu with some personality draws me in, too. If a dish has someone’s name attached to it, odds are it will be worth your time. A Mexican dish on a French menu? It might be there because a Mexican cook made it for the pre-shift “family meal” in the restaurant and his colleagues thought it worth a wider audience. In recent years, the demand for nonalcoholic drinks is up, so I keep a look out for interesting zero-proof selections.

Finally, and most personally, I’m a sucker for dishes that I would likely never make at home (Peking duck, suckling pig, Dover sole) and those that flag in their makeup any of the following: anchovies, almonds, butterscotch, goat cheese, lemon, thyme and meringue. (Love me a classic île flottante, or “floating island.”)

I’m looking for a solid restaurant with a view in the city. 

Look no further than Limani, the dashing, three-floor Greek oasis whose picture windows capture boats, water and more at The Wharf in SW D.C. The airy white interior with accents of blue makes me feel cooler just walking in, and I appreciate the consistency of the cooking. When opening executive chef Lonnie Zoeller died unexpectedly last year, his sous chef, Antonio Contreras, ably slipped into his place in the kitchen.
DC0A8329 copy.jpg (10898x7812, AR: 1.40)A meal this month reminded me of my first visit to Limani. Fried in a kettle of olive oil, the signature stack of thin, hand-cut eggplant and zucchini arrives glossy but greaseless — also hot, crisp and cooled with a dip of tzatziki. (Move over, potato chips.) Bite into the supple grilled squid and out rushes a river of tangy cheese. Loup de mer is cooked head-on, then simply brightened with capers and lemon. A trio of lamb chops is as succulent as I remember, too, and don’t be surprised when a server in a white jacket delivers a gratis gift to the table. (My party received a strawberry pavlova to share.)

“Our way to show Greek hospitality is to send something out for free,” says general manager Michael Deery. He says there’s a word for it: philoxenia, translated as “love of strangers.” The welcoming approach extends to meal deals, including three courses for $39 at lunch.

Limani originated on Long Island and begat branches in Manhattan, Charlotte as well as D.C. The last spreads comfort and sunshine across more than 16,000 square feet and can seat more than 600 people. It’s a big place with a big heart.

What do you think of servers who use “you guys” as a greeting at the table? 

No bother if it’s me and some other men in, say, a bar or someplace relaxed.

But I know, because readers have complained to me repeatedly over the years, that a lot of people object to the overly familiar, too-casual patter. “You guys” overlooks women in the mix. It can also sound unprofessional to some ears (vintage ears, in particular), especially in upscale settings.

The better-for-everyone approach is to avoid calling anyone anything. Ditch the pronouns. It’s hard to argue with “Welcome, and thanks for joining us.”
entries.author: Tom Sietsema

entries.title: Postal Officials Say Trump’s Mail-Ballot Push Will Create Widespread Errors
entries.summary: USPS has just weeks to implement a rule ahead of the November midterms.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s push to have the U.S. Postal Service screen voters for eligibility in the midterm election is running up against tight deadlines that some officials are warning will cause massive errors and disenfranchisement.

The Supreme Court this week temporarily allowed the Postal Service to move forward with a new plan — based on a Trump executive order — that would require states to submit lists of their eligible voters to the mailing agency, which would then ensure no ballots are mailed to individuals not on those lists.

While the rule faces several renewed legal challenges, USPS now has just weeks until some states begin sending out ballots ahead of the November elections, and it has to bring thousands of state and local offices up to speed on the new steps.

USPS has proposed something it has never done before, which would require a heavy lift, said Tom Day, a Postal Service executive for 35 years who spent parts of his career personally responsible for developing the network technology the agency would need to carry out its rule.

“This is not something where you just flip the switch and turn it on,” said Day, an appointed member of the Postal Regulatory Commission since 2023. “I don’t know how the hell they’re going to do it.”

Under Trump’s order, the agency must develop a process to cross-reference all outgoing ballots against still-to-be-submitted lists from states. While the Postal Service has for decades automated the processing of mail and reading of addresses, it has not used those capabilities to pick out mailers ineligible to use its network.

While states will maintain full control over who is on their eligibility lists, a final regulation put forward last week calls on USPS to do exactly that.

The Postal Service is currently working on technical solutions to implement the rule, according to a source familiar with the planning, who added that the agency is focusing on ensuring its review of mailed ballots against state-provided lists is error-free.

Day, however, said that was an impossible goal and erroneously denied ballots are inevitable.

“No system works at 100% accuracy,” he said.

The Postal Service typically would spend at least a year rolling out a new system like the one that will be required for ballot screening, hold a conference for all impacted jurisdictions and provide training to 8,000 election boards around the country, Day said.

He noted that without all of those steps, and with some states sending out ballots as soon as early September, he expects a 20% to 30% error rate, “and that would be a disaster.”

“We haven’t run the tests to give us the validity that the damn thing will work,” Day said. “To do it in three weeks, my God, there’s no way.”

Another senior postal official said the agency was placing significant burdens on states, an argument many states have made in federal court.

“We’re getting near Labor Day here,” the official said. “Just the uncertainty, I can only imagine trying to be a state election official. What can you do?”

The city of Madison, Wisconsin, and Travis County, Texas, in conjunction with outside groups, told a federal court on Tuesday that the Postal Service lacks sufficient staff to answer questions from jurisdictions around the country on the new process, alleging USPS employs just 40 specialized analysts to field those inquiries.

“Unanswered questions in this context risk disenfranchising voters,” they said in court filings.

They added that USPS must train tens of thousands of clerks, who previously have only received instruction on how to identify ballots and expedite their delivery, rather than on refusing to accept them.

In its final rule, the Postal Service said it would train its analysts and provide “additional resources as necessary” to ensure customers receive consistent and accurate advice.

The Postal Service said it will use a “straightforward” process to verify ballots are eligible for distribution, in part by requiring election officials to physically drop them off at designated points or post offices and stand and wait while they are checked. In their lawsuits, local officials suggested that plan was unworkable and would take an unrealistic amount of time.

The agency acknowledged, in response to comments on its proposed rule, that it was requiring states to adjust their processes and incur new costs, but said "any logistical or financial difficulties" and concerns that "immediate implementation would prove impossible" were outweighed by the law-enforcement benefits of the rule. The Postal Service declined to comment for this story.

States, local jurisdictions and advocacy groups are pursuing various legal pathways to stop USPS from implementing the rule. The Supreme Court has ruled only that rulings halting implementation of the executive order were premature before the Postal Service finalized its proposal, which it has now done. Challengers this week updated their lawsuits or filed new ones.

The Postal Service, in the final version of its ballot rule, maintained it has adequate staffing for enforcement and does not need to build new capacity, though it conceded that much of the work to implement the rule still lies ahead of it.

In addition to training staff, USPS still must develop guidance documents, the agency said in its regulatory filing, to make clear how to create an account to upload voter lists to its portal, assign users, properly format files and resolve errors.

USPS said it anticipated that states would continually update their lists, meaning its database of eligible voters will be evolving up until Election Day.

The uncertainty still remaining shows that the agency is creating a “unique process that USPS hasn’t done before,” the senior postal official said.

“If it was so easy, the Postal Service could point to, ‘Here’s how we already do it,’” the official said. “It raises questions.”

In a response to a separate challenge before the Postal Regulatory Commission, the Postal Service said the new rule was not entirely novel, likening it to regulations for mailing certain animals or electronic cigarettes, and that it was similar to standards it has for allowing cremated remains or replica explosives to enter the mailstream. It also told its regulator that voters would not see any direct disruption to their experience with the mail.

David Steiner, the U.S. postmaster general, previously told Congress that any state that does not submit its voter lists to his agency would be prohibited from using mailed ballots. States must also conform to new requirements for envelope and barcode design, though officials stressed that USPS has pushed for those standards for years and that many states already comply with them.

In the meantime, the Department of Homeland Security is, as required by Trump’s order, working with the Social Security Administration and State Department to provide data to states on eligible voters to help them compile their own lists.

NOTUS previously reported that DHS in June was still working on back-end development and initial testing for that data sharing. The databases it was tapping into were unreliable for the project of verifying voter eligibility, former federal officials said, and could also lead to large-scale errors.
